one.title: The Lost Java Treasure
one.subtitle: A Five-Room Treasure Hunt
one.congratulatoryMessage: Treasure found! You recovered all three scroll clues.
one.missionTitle: MISSION: Find the Lost Java Treasure
one.missionText: The treasure has been sealed away. Explore the rooms, survive the obstacles, collect the three hidden scrolls, and reach the treasure.

questions.formattedQuestion:
FINAL TREASURE RIDDLE
I can hold numbers, but I am not a number. I have a name, and my value can change. What am I?
riddleVariants: I can hold numbers, but I am not a number. I have a name, and my value can change. What am I?
Java gives me a name so a value can be stored, read, and changed later. What am I?
I am a named container in a program that can remember a score, message, or other value. What am I?
My name stays recognizable while the information I contain may change as a program runs. What am I?
A programmer declares me before assigning data that the code needs to remember. What am I?
I provide a reusable name for a piece of stored information in Java. What am I?
questions.prompt: I can hold numbers, but I am not a number. I have a name, and my value can change. What am I? Jumbled word: AIBLERVE
hints: The scrolls describe a named container whose value can change.
Unscramble AIBLERVE.
questions.successText: Correct! The Lost Java Treasure is yours.
questions.failureText: The chest remains sealed. Use the three scroll clues and try again.

rooms.objective: Mission introduction: time the moving platform, cross the blinking bridge, avoid the elemental's fire, and reach the exit.
Collect 2 keys, avoid the minion, find Scroll #1, and enter the unlocked exit.

coins.clueText: A program can give a reusable name to stored information so it can find and use that value again later.

rooms.objective: Avoid the spikes, use the Jump Boost for the raised path, collect Scroll #2, and exit.

coins.clueText: Stored information may be a number, word, or truth value, and it can be updated while the program runs.

rooms.objective: Ride the moving platform, avoid the two minions, collect the Shield and Scroll #3, and exit.

coins.clueText: Use a named storage place when code must remember a score, price, message, or other value for later instructions.

rooms.objective: Final stage: combine careful jumps and spikes, then reach the Treasure Chest.

one.title: Temple of Data Types
one.subtitle: Discover What Kinds of Values Java Can Store
one.congratulatoryMessage: DATA TEMPLE RESTORED! You discovered that Java uses data types to identify the kind of information a variable can store.
one.missionText: The Lost Java Treasure revealed an ancient temple. Collect three hidden learning scrolls, then use their clues to unlock the Data Core.

questions.formattedQuestion:
FINAL TREASURE RIDDLE
I tell Java what kind of value can be stored. I can describe whole numbers, decimals, truth values, or text. What am I?
riddleVariants: I tell Java what kind of value can be stored. I can describe whole numbers, decimals, truth values, or text. What am I?
I classify information as int, double, boolean, String, or another kind Java understands. What am I?
Before Java stores a value, I describe the form of data that belongs in its container. What am I?
I determine whether a Java value represents a whole number, decimal, truth value, or text. What am I?
Java uses me to know which operations and values are valid for stored information. What am I?
I am the category assigned to data so Java knows how that information should be handled. What am I?
questions.prompt: I tell Java what kind of value can be stored. I can describe whole numbers, decimals, truth values, or text. What am I? Jumbled word: ATAD EPYT
hints: Review what int, double, boolean, and String have in common.
Unscramble ATAD EPYT.
failureMessages: Incorrect. Review the three scroll clues and try again.
Incorrect. Think about what tells Java what kind of value is being stored.
The Data Core remains sealed. Return to the checkpoint and try again.
questions.successText: Correct! The Data Core is restored.

rooms.objective: Number Chamber: find Scroll #1 to learn about whole and decimal numbers.
Truth Chamber: find Scroll #2 to learn about true and false values.
Text Chamber: find Scroll #3 to learn how Java stores text.
Mixed Data Trial: combine boosts and moving platforms to reach the Data Core.
Data Core: survive the final chamber and unlock the treasure using all three scroll clues.

one.title: Fortress of Operators
one.subtitle: Learn How Java Works with Values
one.congratulatoryMessage: OPERATOR FORTRESS RESTORED! You discovered how Java uses operators to calculate, compare, and evaluate information.
one.missionText: The path leads to an ancient fortress where Java's Operator Seals have been scattered. Recover the seals, uncover their meaning, and restore the fortress core.

questions.formattedQuestion:
FINAL TREASURE RIDDLE
I am a symbol that tells Java to perform an action on one or more values. I can calculate, compare, or test conditions. What am I?
riddleVariants: I am a symbol that tells Java to perform an action on one or more values. I can calculate, compare, or test conditions. What am I?
Symbols such as +, ==, and && are examples of me because I make Java act on values. What am I?
I stand between or before values to perform arithmetic, comparison, or logical work. What am I?
Java uses me to add numbers, compare results, and combine conditions. What am I?
I may be arithmetic, relational, or logical, and I tell an expression what action to perform. What am I?
Without me, Java expressions could not calculate, compare, or test their operands. What am I?
questions.prompt: I am a symbol that tells Java to perform an action on one or more values. I can calculate, compare, or test conditions. What am I? Jumbled word: RATOPERO
hints: Review the three operator scroll clues.
Think about symbols used to calculate, compare, and test conditions.
failureMessages: Incorrect. Review the three scroll clues and try again.
Incorrect. Think about the symbols Java uses to calculate, compare, and test conditions.
The Operator Core remains sealed. Return to the checkpoint and try again.
questions.successText: Correct! The Operator Core is restored.

rooms.objective: Comparison Split: take the moving upper route for the Seal and collapsing lower route for Scroll #2.

coins.clueText:
COMPARISON OPERATORS
==  !=  >  <  >=  <=

Two values can be compared to discover whether they are equal, different, greater, or less.

portal.lockedMessage: Portal Locked — Recover the Comparison Seal and Scroll #2.

rooms.objective: Arithmetic Gauntlet: recover the Seal from the moving route, then risk the collapsing ledge for Scroll #1.

coins.clueText:
ARITHMETIC OPERATORS
+  -  *  /  %

Some symbols add, subtract, multiply, divide, or reveal what remains.

portal.lockedMessage: Portal Locked — Recover the Arithmetic Seal and Scroll #1.

rooms.objective: Logic Circuit: use the timed lifts and disappearing high route to recover the Logical Seal and Scroll #3.

coins.clueText:
LOGICAL OPERATORS
&&  ||  !

Some conditions must both be true, some need only one truth, and some reverse the answer entirely.

portal.lockedMessage: Portal Locked — Recover the Logical Seal and Scroll #3.

rooms.objective: Operator Trial: cross the hazard route and reach the portal.
Operator Core: survive the collapsing ascent, recover the risky heart and shield, then reach the treasure.

one.title: Citadel of Decisions
one.subtitle: Java Conditional Statements
one.congratulatoryMessage: CITADEL OF DECISIONS AWAKENED! You discovered how Java evaluates conditions and chooses which code should execute.
one.missionText: Beyond the Operator Fortress lies a citadel of branching paths. Its gates respond only to the correct conditions. Follow the clues, choose wisely, and awaken the Decision Core.

questions.prompt: Is score >= 5 true when score is 10?
Which path executes when coins is 3 and the condition is coins >= 5?
questions.successText: Correct! Java follows the ELSE path.
questions.failureText: That condition is false. Choose the path Java would execute.

questions.formattedQuestion:
int score = 82;
Gate A: score >= 90
Gate B: score >= 75
Gate C: else
questions.prompt: For score = 82, which branch is selected first?
questions.successText: Correct! Gate B is the first true branch.
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Evaluate the conditions from top to bottom.

questions.prompt: Will the if block execute when health is 8 and health > 5?
Which branch executes when keys is 1 and keys >= 2?

questions.formattedQuestion:
int score = 70;
>= 90: Gold
>= 75: Silver
>= 60: Bronze
else: No Reward
questions.prompt: For score = 70, which result does Java choose?

questions.formattedQuestion:
FINAL TREASURE RIDDLE
Java checks me before deciding which path to follow. I can be true or false, and the result determines which code will execute. What am I?
riddleVariants: Java checks me before deciding which path to follow. I can be true or false, and the result determines which code will execute. What am I?
I am evaluated as true or false before an if statement chooses whether its block should run. What am I?
A decision in Java depends on my truth value before selecting a branch. What am I?
I am the test written inside parentheses that controls an if, else-if, or loop. What am I?
When Java reaches a decision point, it evaluates me to choose the next path. What am I?
Comparisons and logical expressions form me, and my result is either true or false. What am I?
questions.prompt: Java checks me before deciding which path to follow. I can be true or false. What am I? Jumbled word: NODIITCON
hints: Review the three conditional scroll clues.
Think about what Java checks before choosing a path.
failureMessages: Incorrect. Review the three scroll clues and try again.
Incorrect. Think about what Java checks before choosing which path to execute.
The Decision Core remains sealed. Return to the checkpoint and try again.

rooms.objective: The IF Chamber: recover the IF Seal and Scroll #1, then enter the portal.

coins.clueText:
IF STATEMENT

An if statement runs code when its condition is true.

When the condition is true, the path ahead will open.

portal.lockedMessage: Recover the IF Seal and Scroll #1.

rooms.objective: The ELSE Chamber: recover the ELSE Seal and Scroll #2, then enter the portal.

coins.clueText:
ELSE STATEMENT

Else provides another path when the if condition is false.

When one path refuses to open, another may be waiting.

portal.lockedMessage: Recover the ELSE Seal and Scroll #2.

rooms.objective: The ELSE-IF Chamber: recover the final seal and Scroll #3, then enter the portal.

coins.clueText:
ELSE IF

Else-if tests another condition when the previous condition is false.

Java checks conditions in order until one becomes true.

portal.lockedMessage: Recover the ELSE-IF Seal and Scroll #3.

rooms.objective: Decision Trial: cross the rising cave arch and reach the Decision Core portal.
Decision Core: survive the final route and unlock the treasure using all three scroll clues.

one.title: Labyrinth of Loops
one.subtitle: Java Loops
one.congratulatoryMessage: THE ENDLESS CYCLE IS BROKEN! You mastered Java's loops and discovered how programs can repeat instructions efficiently.
one.missionText: The path has led to an ancient labyrinth trapped in an endless cycle. Its mechanisms repeat again and again. Master Java's loops, recover the Loop Seals, and break the cycle.

questions.formattedQuestion:
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)

How many times will this loop run?
questions.prompt: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) run?
questions.successText: Correct! The FOR Loop Gate opens.
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Count the values of i and try again.

questions.prompt: When will the loop stop?
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Trace the loop and try again.

questions.prompt: Will this do-while loop body execute?
questions.successText: Correct! A do-while body executes before checking.
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Remember when a do-while checks its condition.

questions.prompt: How many times does for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) execute?
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Trace the loop and try again.

questions.prompt: What is the final value of x?
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Trace the loop and try again.

questions.prompt: How many times does the loop body execute?
questions.failureText: Incorrect. Trace the loop and try again.

questions.formattedQuestion:
FINAL TREASURE RIDDLE
I make Java repeat instructions without writing the same code again and again. I may repeat a set number of times or continue while a condition is true. What am I?
riddleVariants: I make Java repeat instructions without writing the same code again and again. I may repeat a set number of times or continue while a condition is true. What am I?
I run a block of code repeatedly, either for a known count or while a test remains true. What am I?
For, while, and do-while are three forms of me in Java. What am I?
I save programmers from copying the same instructions whenever an action must repeat. What am I?
My cycle continues according to a counter or condition until it is time to stop. What am I?
Java enters me to execute the same block across multiple iterations. What am I?
questions.prompt: What makes Java repeat instructions? Jumbled word: OPOL
hints: Review the three loop scroll clues.
Think about what Java uses to repeat instructions.
failureMessages: Incorrect. Review the three scroll clues and try again.
Incorrect. Think about what Java uses to repeat instructions.
The Endless Core remains sealed. Return to the checkpoint and try again.
questions.successText: Correct! The Endless Core cycle is broken.

rooms.objective: The FOR Loop Chamber: recover the FOR Seal and Scroll #1, then enter the portal.

coins.clueText:
FOR LOOP

A for loop repeats code using a starting value, condition, and update.

When repetitions are known, the path can be counted from beginning to end.

portal.lockedMessage: Recover the FOR Seal and Scroll #1.

rooms.objective: The WHILE Chamber: recover the WHILE Seal and Scroll #2, then enter the portal.

coins.clueText:
WHILE LOOP

A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains true.

The cycle continues while the condition remains true.

portal.lockedMessage: Recover the WHILE Seal and Scroll #2.

rooms.objective: The DO-WHILE Chamber: recover the final seal and Scroll #3, then enter the portal.

coins.clueText:
DO-WHILE LOOP

A do-while loop executes first and checks its condition afterward.

Some cycles begin before asking whether they should continue.

portal.lockedMessage: Recover the DO-WHILE Seal and Scroll #3.

rooms.objective: Loop Trial: cross the repeating platform pattern and reach the Endless Core.
The Endless Core: time the repeating platforms and hazards, then unlock the Loop Core Treasure.

hints: int uses 32 bits.
The range is roughly ±2 billion.

float can only hold positive numbers
float is an integer type internally
float values cannot be compared with ==

hints: Think about how 0.1 is stored in binary.
Use BigDecimal for money calculations instead.

The original object is always destroyed after the call
Objects cannot be passed as method parameters

Mutating fields on the object works; pointing the parameter at a new object does not affect the original.

question.prompt: What is the difference between a runtime error and a logic error?

Logic errors are always caught by the compiler

hints: Logic errors are silent — the program runs but gives wrong answers.
Runtime errors throw exceptions that stop execution.

question.prompt: What is the main drawback of using a wildcard import like import java.util.*;?

options.label: It hides which specific classes are used, making code harder to read and maintain
It causes a compile error if any class in the package is missing
It imports private inner classes too
It significantly slows down compilation

hints: * imports every public class in the package.
Readers cannot tell which classes are actually used.
question.explanation: Wildcard imports pull in all public classes from a package. While convenient, they obscure which classes are actually used, and can cause ambiguity if two packages define a class with the same name.

question.prompt: What is the difference between a runtime error and a logic error?

options.label: A runtime error crashes the program; a logic error produces wrong output without crashing
Runtime errors are syntax mistakes; logic errors crash the program
Both cause the program to crash in the same way
Logic errors are always caught by the compiler

hints: Logic errors are silent — the program runs but gives wrong answers.
Runtime errors throw exceptions that stop execution.
question.explanation: Runtime errors (e.g. NullPointerException) crash the program with an exception. Logic errors let the program run to completion but produce incorrect results — they are often harder to find because there is no error message.

question.prompt: What is the main drawback of using a wildcard import like import java.util.*;?

It imports private inner classes too
It significantly slows down compilation

hints: * imports every public class in the package.
Readers cannot tell which classes are actually used.
question.explanation: Wildcard imports pull in all public classes from a package. While convenient, they obscure which classes are actually used, and can cause ambiguity if two packages define a class with the same name.

question.prompt: Why does Java not support extending multiple classes?

options.label: Multiple inheritance can cause ambiguity (the diamond problem) when two parents define the same method
It is technically impossible in all languages
Java allows it only for abstract classes
It would slow runtime performance too much

hints: What happens if both parents have a method with the same name?
Java uses interfaces to achieve multiple-type behavior instead.
question.explanation: Multiple class inheritance leads to the diamond problem: if two parents both define the same method, the subclass has no unambiguous method to inherit. Java solves this by allowing only single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation.

question.prompt: What is the difference between compile-time and runtime polymorphism in Java?

Compile-time polymorphism only works with primitive types

question.prompt: What is a key difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?

options.label: An abstract class can have fields and concrete methods; an interface's methods are abstract by default (pre-Java 8)
An interface can be instantiated; an abstract class cannot
Abstract classes support multiple inheritance; interfaces do not
An interface must extend an abstract class

hints: An abstract class is still a class — it can have state.
An interface is a pure contract with no state (before Java 8 default methods).
question.explanation: An abstract class can have instance fields, constructors, and both abstract and concrete methods. A traditional interface only declares method signatures (a contract). Java 8+ added default methods to interfaces.
